name: Distributed Home Grid as Outage Insurance
deck: As grid reliability deteriorated in 2024-2026 due to increasing demand, aging infrastructure, and extreme weather, household solar-and-storage systems pivoted from a cost-savings narrative to an outage-insurance and energy-resilience story. Sunrun exemplified this shift: storage-attachment rates climbed from 71% in Q4 2025 to 74% in Q2 2026, and management reframed the business around 'protecting families from rising utility costs and an increasingly unreliable grid' and 'building a distributed power plant.' The trend showed that residential energy systems are now being sold and purchased as much for reliability and peace-of-mind as for electricity cost reduction. This reshaping of consumer demand created new monetization layers (grid services, distributed power-plant participation, home-to-grid programs) and strengthened customer retention.
core_bet: Household energy resilience, driven by rising outage frequency and grid stress, will sustain solar-and-storage attachment and create recurring service relationships that capture more value than one-time hardware sales. Companies that frame the offering as 'distributed power plant' rather than 'cheaper electricity' will command higher lifetime value and lower churn.

mechanism: Grid reliability events (PSPS events in California 2023-2024, extreme heat-driven demand spikes in Texas/Southwest 2025-2026, infrastructure failures in multiple states) created visible outage anxiety among residential customers. Solar-plus-storage systems offer backup power and bill reduction combined.

Sunrun's business model captures multiple revenue streams from a single installed base: customer subscription revenue (home energy system lease), equipment sales, grid-services monetization (demand response, backup capacity), and potential future distributed power-plant participation. This multi-layering justifies higher customer lifetime value and supports lower churn.

Storage attachment as a product strategy accelerated because batteries complement solar's intermittency and provide outage resilience. The jump from 71% (Q4 2025) to 74% (Q2 2026) storage attachment reflects both improved customer preference (perceived reliability value) and Sunrun's commercial success selling batteries as an add-on to solar systems.
why_now: The inflection was primarily 2024-2026, driven by visible grid stress in California (PSPS events), Texas (extreme summer demand), and the Southwest (aging coal retirements). These events entered mainstream consumer awareness. Simultaneously, battery costs declined and technology improved, making residential storage economically viable. Sunrun's investor materials and guidance in 2025-2026 increasingly emphasized 'protecting families from an increasingly unreliable grid' and 'distributed power plant' language, showing that management recognized the outage-insurance narrative was becoming primary. The Q2 2026 reduced guidance (ASV $4.6-4.9B from $4.8-5.2B prior) was blamed on affiliate-channel softness and direct-sales ramp delays, not demand weakness, suggesting the consumer demand for the system was intact even if sales channels faced friction.
who_pays: Homeowners in regions with outage risk (California, Texas, Southwest) and those with high grid-price escalation (Hawaii, California). Customers pay through lease agreements, equipment purchases, and subscription revenue capture.
who_profits: Sunrun and competitors (Vivint Solar, Tesla Energy) gain recurring revenue from installed bases and subscription economics. Utilities may face eroding peak-load pricing power if distributed storage proliferates. Grid operators gain backup capacity and demand-response capability.
tension: The tension is between Sunrun's subscription-and-services narrative (justify high customer lifetime value) and the physical reality of declining solar generation during extended outages. A multi-day grid outage would expose the limits of residential battery capacity (typically 8-16 kWh, sufficient for hours not days). If customer expectations of outage protection exceed system capability, satisfaction and retention could suffer.
surprising_part: Sunrun's cash-generation guidance was reduced in Q2 2026 (full-year guidance lowered to $200-375M from $250-450M), yet storage attachment rates continued climbing and customer additions remained positive. This decoupling of near-term cash guidance from customer-stack metrics suggests that Sunrun (and investors) believe the long-term customer-value stack and subscription economics are more important than near-term project-finance timing. This inversion—guidance down, customer metrics up—is unusual and reflects confidence in the business model's durability despite short-term capital-structure noise.
one_sentence: Grid reliability anxiety drove residential solar-plus-storage adoption from a cost-savings story to an outage-insurance and distributed-power narrative, enabling recurring subscription and services monetization.
societal_stake: Residential energy resilience and grid reliability for households. If distributed storage proliferates, it could reduce peak-load pressure on aging grids. If it concentrates in affluent neighborhoods, it could exacerbate energy equity divides.

evidence.fact: Q2 2026 revenue $870M, Aggregate Subscriber Value $1.175B, Contracted Net Earning Assets $3.677B. Storage attachment rate 74% (up from 71% Q4 2025), networked storage capacity 4.647 GWh, customers 1.206M. Q2 customer additions 20,979, but full-year ASV guidance reduced to $4.6-4.9B from prior $4.8-5.2B due to affiliate-channel and direct-sales channel friction. Full-year 2025 revenue $2.957B, cash flow $377M, ASV $1.278B, storage attachment 71%.
